conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You’re here because of abdominal pain and vomiting. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the pain has been coming back like it has before—crampy, all over my belly. I’ve been nauseous and threw up a couple times. I also feel really dehydrated—my mouth is dry and my urine is dark.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We saw in your imaging that there’s no bowel obstruction, but your colon is quite full of stool. This could be contributing to the discomfort. We also hooked your G-tube to gravity drainage to help relieve pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds familiar. I’ve had this before with my fibrosing mesenteritis. Is that what’s going on again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it looks like a flare of your fibrosing mesenteritis. We’re giving you IV fluids for dehydration and medications for pain and nausea. We started with IV morphine and ketorolac, but I understand the ketorolac didn’t help much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, the morphine helps more with the pain. I’m glad we’re not using Compazine—I’m allergic to that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve noted your allergies—Compazine, Dilaudid, and several others. We’re using promethazine instead for nausea, which should be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my G-tube is draining okay? I felt some relief after it was hooked up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it drained about 1,450 cc overnight—that’s a good amount. It helps reduce the pressure in your stomach and intestines. We’ll keep it to gravity for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. I’ve been so worried about another blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But the imaging shows no blockage—just a lot of stool in the lower colon. No free air, so no sign of perforation. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What about my potassium? I saw it was low in the lab results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your potassium was 3.2, which is a bit low. We’re giving you potassium supplements in your IV fluids to bring it up safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ve had that before. It makes me feel weak when it’s low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll keep monitoring it. Now, your liver enzymes are also a bit elevated—ALT and AST are higher than usual. We did an ultrasound this morning to check your liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Because of my hepatitis C? I’ve had that for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s likely the main cause. The ultrasound showed fatty infiltration of the liver, which can happen with chronic hepatitis C. It doesn’t show cirrhosis or serious damage, but you should follow up with your GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. Should I be worried about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not acutely, but it’s important to monitor. Fatty liver can progress if not managed. Your primary doctor or GI specialist can help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll make sure to follow up. What about my blood thinner? I’m on warfarin for my DVT history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Your INR was low—only 1.6—so you weren’t fully protected against clots. We’ve started you on Lovenox injections to bridge until your INR comes back up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve done that before. How long will I need the shots?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just until your INR is stable above 2. We’ll check it again tomorrow. Once it’s in range, you can go back to warfarin alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. The pain is much less, and I haven’t felt nauseous since yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your INR is now 2.2, which is in the safe range, so we’ll stop the Lovenox and continue warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Can I start eating again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re going to start you on a soft diet. We’ll begin with clear liquids and advance as tolerated. Your G-tube can stay clamped for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m really looking forward to eating something. What about my pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll switch you from IV morphine to your regular oral morphine. You can still use the liquid form as needed for breakthrough pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds—like metoclopramide and ranitidine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can restart all your usual medications. We’ll make sure your discharge list matches what you were on before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. You ate dinner last night without any issues, and your labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much stronger. Am I going home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re planning to discharge you today. Your pain is controlled, you’re eating well, and your INR is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Any instructions for when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue eating small, moderate meals. Stay on your regular meds. Watch for worsening pain, vomiting, or inability to tolerate food—those would be reasons to call your doctor or return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the liver ultrasound results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, follow up with your primary care doctor or GI specialist in the next two weeks to discuss the fatty liver changes and your hepatitis C.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for taking such good care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready, and you should be home within a few hours.
